prayer.text: Saint Benedict of Nursia, pray for us.

cues.text: Fleeing a Decaying Capital
Born around 480 at Nursia in central Italy to a family of some standing, Benedict was sent to Rome as a young man to pursue the classical education expected of his class.

What he found there instead disillusioned him utterly: a city of moral decadence and declining discipline that struck the young student as fundamentally incompatible with the serious spiritual life he was beginning to long for.
Benedict abandoned his studies and withdrew from the city entirely, eventually settling alone in a remote cave near Subiaco .
Guided secretly by a nearby monk who lowered food to him on a rope, he spent three years in solitary prayer, penance, and spiritual formation, deliberately hidden from the world he had left behind.
A Reluctant Abbot, and an Attempt on His Life
Benedict's reputation for holiness spread despite his own desire for obscurity, and a nearby community of monks, left without a leader, eventually persuaded him to become their abbot.
The arrangement proved disastrous: Benedict's strict standards clashed sharply with the monks' looser habits.
According to St. Gregory the Great 's account of his life, some grew so resentful that they attempted to poison him with wine and bread.
The cup shattered when Benedict made the sign of the cross over it; tradition holds, a raven carried away the poisoned loaf before he could eat it.

Rather than remain among men so unwilling to be led, Benedict returned to his solitude, and disciples soon gathered around him there instead, organized eventually into twelve small monasteries of twelve monks each.
A Temple Overthrown at Monte Cassino

Around the year 529, Benedict moved south to Monte Cassino , a hilltop still crowned by an ancient pagan temple to Apollo where local country people, Gregory tells us, continued to offer sacrifice according to old custom.
Benedict destroyed the idol, overturned the altar, and set the surrounding sacred groves ablaze.

In their place, he built an oratory dedicated to St. Martin—a deliberate, physical act of consecrating pagan ground to Christian worship that would become the mother house of the entire Benedictine order.
A Rule of Balance and Moderation
At Monte Cassino, in his matured spiritual and administrative wisdom, Benedict composed the Rule that bears his name.
It was not an extreme or crushing code of austerity, but a remarkably balanced, humane pattern of life ordered around prayer, sacred reading, and manual labor.
Later generations would sum up his spirituality in the phrase ora et labora , "pray and work."
Earlier monastic legislators had often demanded heroic feats of individual asceticism.
Benedict's genius lay in designing a Rule any ordinary, imperfect person could actually live.
It was moderate in its demands, attentive to each monk's strengths and weaknesses, and organized around shared life's steady, unspectacular rhythm rather than a solitary hero's isolated struggles.
A Twin Sister, and a Peaceful Death

Tradition, accepted by the Venerable Bede, holds that Benedict had a twin sister, St. Scholastica , herself consecrated to religious life, whom he continued to visit once a year for a day of shared prayer and conversation until her death.
Benedict himself died at Monte Cassino around 547 and was buried, fittingly, in the same tomb as his sister.
Two lives bound by blood and shared, lifelong devotion to God rested together at the end, as they had so often prayed together across the years.
Legacy
Benedict's Rule, copied and carried across Europe by generations of monks, became the single most influential template for Western monastic life.
This occurred even as barbarian invasions and political collapse swept away much of the old Roman world.

Benedictine monasteries would go on to preserve classical learning, teach agriculture, and anchor Christian civilization across the whole continent through the centuries historians once called the Dark Ages.
Declared Patron of Europe by Pope Paul VI in 1964, Benedict remains a quiet, enduring testament.
Much can grow from one young man's simple decision to leave a decaying city.
He sought, instead of worldly advancement, nothing more than solitude with God.
